content: 1. All sample types collected and described in the guidance should undergo thorough testing. Any findings from metagenomic analyses, particularly the detection of pathogens, must be confirmed using additional laboratory techniques such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR) or whole genome sequencing (WGS). The interpretation of metagenomic testing results should be carefully considered, taking into account the timing of sample collection and the patient’s symptoms. 2. Data collection should include detailed information to support the analysis of findings. This includes the type of specimen, specimen identification, date and time of collection, date of symptom onset, and details of any treatments administered to the patient prior to or during specimen collection. Additional information on the sequencing and data analysis workflow should also be documented. 3. Since the cause of the event is currently unknown, all specimen handling should follow a risk-based approach. Each laboratory must conduct a local institutional risk assessment. Core biosafety requirements must be adhered to when handling specimens, and enhanced control measures should be implemented based on the risk assessment. For further details on biosafety requirements and control measures, refer to the fourth edition of the WHO Laboratory Biosafety Manual (LBM4). 4. Various commercial kits are available for pathogen detection as described in the guidance. However, some may require in-house assays. Not all commercial kits are licensed or approved in all countries or by stringent international regulatory authorities. Some kits may be approved for in vitro diagnostics (IVD) for clinical purposes, while others may be approved for research use only (RUO). Information on commercial kits is readily available online. WHO provides a list of prequalified diagnostics for Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, and HIV testing, as well as a list of assessed assays for SARS-CoV-2 under the Emergency Use Listing. For other diagnostics, WHO does not endorse specific products, and laboratories are encouraged to independently determine the suitability and regulatory approval status of kits for their specific needs. 5. Laboratories must comply with national reporting requirements for cases and test results. Member States are strongly encouraged to identify, investigate, and report potential cases of severe acute hepatitis of unknown etiology in children. Core epidemiological and risk factor information should be collected and submitted to WHO through agreed reporting mechanisms, which may vary by region. Reporting through International Health Regulations (2005) channels is also an option. Notifications should include details of the specific assays performed. WHO encourages the sharing of genetic sequence data through publicly accessible databases. Laboratory results should be interpreted alongside clinical and epidemiological information. A clinical case report form is available for use. 6. Access to timely and accurate testing of samples from cases under investigation is critical for surveillance. All countries should have access to reliable testing, either domestically or through international laboratories willing and able to perform the required diagnostic testing. WHO, through its regional offices, can assist Member States in accessing testing and metagenomic analysis internationally if needed. Member States may consider signing material transfer agreements (MTAs) with international referral laboratories to address issues such as ownership of clinical material and intellectual property rights before shipping specimens. 7. This updated interim guidance was developed by the WHO steering group for laboratory and diagnostic stakeholders across national public health authorities. It incorporates the currently available information. Laboratory testing for severe acute hepatitis of unknown etiology in children is an ongoing area of focus. WHO will continue to monitor the situation closely and issue updates if necessary. Otherwise, this interim guidance will expire one year after its publication date. 8. Contributors to this guidance include experts from WHO headquarters, regional offices, and other organizations. The work was funded by the WHO Global HIV, Hepatitis, and STI Programmes and the Health Emergencies Programme. For references, consult the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, Public Health England, and the United Kingdom Health Security Agency, among others.
